issues.legal_issue: A High Court deciding a second appeal cannot reappreciate the evidence and overturn concurrent factual findings unless a substantial question of law arises and a recognized ground for interference is established.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both found, after considering the evidence, that the disputed properties had not been blended with joint family property.
The High Court reconsidered the evidence and reversed those concurrent findings while deciding the second appeals.

The Supreme Court found that the questions framed by the High Court were not substantial questions of law and that the lower courts’ findings were not shown to be perverse or contrary to the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of its second-appellate jurisdiction; its judgment was set aside and the trial court’s dismissal of the suits was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a second appeal requires a substantial question of law, and the High Court cannot substitute its view for that of the first appellate court merely by reappreciating evidence. Interference with factual findings may be justified where material evidence was not considered or inadmissible evidence was relied on, or where the findings are otherwise legally erroneous, including being contrary to mandatory law or the law declared by the Supreme Court, or based on no evidence. The Court relied on Panchugopal Barua v. Umesh Chandra Goswami, Kondiba Dagadu Kadam v. Savitribai Sopan Gujar, and Ishwar Dass Jain v. Sohan Lal.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_evidence_based_findings and high_court_reappreciated_evidence and not recognized_ground_for_interference and questions_not_substantial_law

predicates.second_appeal: The matter came before the High Court in a second appeal from decisions of lower courts.
predicates.concurrent_evidence_based_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same factual finding after considering the evidence.
predicates.high_court_reappreciated_evidence: The High Court reconsidered the evidence and reached its own factual conclusion.
predicates.recognized_ground_for_interference: The findings were shown to be legally erroneous, perverse, contrary to governing law, or based on inadmissible or no evidence.
predicates.questions_not_substantial_law: The questions framed for the second appeal concerned facts or ordinary questions of law rather than substantial questions of law.

issues.definition: When a second appeal concerns concurrent evidence-based findings, the High Court reappreciates the evidence, no recognized ground for interference is established, and the questions are not substantial questions of law, interference is impermissible.

issues.legal_issue: A member’s separate or self-acquired property does not become joint family property through family use or support alone; blending requires a clear intention to abandon separate rights and place the property in the common stock.
material_facts: The disputed properties had been received by the father under a settlement from a person who was not his direct male ancestor, and were found to be his self-acquired properties.
The father executed settlement deeds and a will dealing with the properties in favour of one son.
The family members lived together and loans were taken in connection with the properties, but the evidence did not establish a clear intention by the father to abandon his separate rights.
The trial court and the first appellate court found that the properties had not been blended with joint family property.
issues.conclusion: The properties were not proved to have been blended with joint family property, and the High Court was not justified in overturning the lower courts’ findings on that issue.
issues.legal_principle: A separate or self-acquired property of a member of a joint Hindu family may acquire the character of joint family property if its owner voluntarily throws it into the common stock with the intention of abandoning separate rights. That intention must be clearly established; it cannot be inferred merely from allowing family members to use the property or from using its income to support them. The Court applied this settled principle without citing a particular earlier case for it.

rule.if: partition_property_dispute and property_separately_acquired and not clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_rights and (family_use_or_support or family_related_loans)

predicates.partition_property_dispute: The proceeding concerned a claim to divide property said to belong to a joint family.
predicates.property_separately_acquired: The property was acquired separately by an individual rather than received from direct male ancestors as ancestral property.
predicates.clear_intention_to_abandon_separate_righ: The owner clearly intended to give up separate rights in the property and place it in the family common stock.
predicates.family_use_or_support: Other family members used the property or received support from its income.
predicates.family_related_loans: Family members living together took loans connected with the property or its use.

issues.definition: In a property-division dispute, separately acquired property is not treated as joint family property when there is no clear intention to abandon separate rights, even if family members used it or took related loans.
